## Project identity
**Descriptive name:** **ns-3 Moving-STA Wi-Fi Throughput Experiment**

A compact ns-3 C++ simulation with one 802.11n AP and one station moving at 4 m/s, a high-rate UDP client/server flow, MinstrelHT rate control, FlowMonitor statistics and one-second scheduled throughput reporting. It directly connects mobility and Wi-Fi performance in code. However, the periodic “throughput vs time” value divides cumulative received bytes by cumulative elapsed time, so it is a running-average throughput rather than true per-interval instantaneous throughput. The default channel/environment and single-run topology also limit research conclusions.

## 4. Core technical scope
A compact ns-3 C++ simulation with one 802.11n AP and one station moving at 4 m/s, a high-rate UDP client/server flow, MinstrelHT rate control, FlowMonitor statistics and one-second scheduled throughput reporting. It directly connects mobility and Wi-Fi performance in code. However, the periodic “throughput vs time” value divides cumulative received bytes by cumulative elapsed time, so it is a running-average throughput rather than true per-interval instantaneous throughput. The default channel/environment and single-run topology also limit research conclusions.

Directly evidenced scope:

- ns-3 C++
- 802.11n Wi-Fi simulation
- mobility models
- UDP traffic generation
- FlowMonitor
- scheduled simulation callbacks
- throughput/loss calculation
- MinstrelHT rate control

## 23. Engineering decisions and tradeoffs

- **Decision/tradeoff 3 — FlowMonitor result extraction:** FlowMonitor/classifier data are used to isolate destination port 9 and report received bytes/packets, average throughput and packet-loss ratio. This provides inspectable measurement logic.
- **Decision/tradeoff 4 — Running-average versus interval-throughput defect:** `CalculateThroughput()` uses total `rxBytes` divided by `currentTime - 1`. Because the byte counter is cumulative, successive points are cumulative averages, not bytes received during the last one-second window. Calling the table “throughput vs time” can therefore mislead without this distinction.

- **Decision/tradeoff 1 — Wi-Fi topology and mobility model:** The code creates one AP and one STA, configures 802.11n with `MinstrelHtWifiManager`, places the AP at the origin and gives the STA constant velocity of 4 m/s along x. This is direct mobile-wireless simulation evidence.
- **Decision/tradeoff 2 — Traffic generation and offered load:** A UDP client sends 1024-byte packets every 1 ms to the AP from t=1 s to 30 s—about 8.192 Mbit/s payload offered load before protocol overhead. This is a clearly parameterized workload.
- **Decision/tradeoff 3 — FlowMonitor result extraction:** FlowMonitor/classifier data are used to isolate destination port 9 and report received bytes/packets, average throughput and packet-loss ratio. This provides inspectable measurement logic.
- **Decision/tradeoff 4 — Running-average versus interval-throughput defect:** `CalculateThroughput()` uses total `rxBytes` divided by `currentTime - 1`. Because the byte counter is cumulative, successive points are cumulative averages, not bytes received during the last one-second window. Calling the table “throughput vs time” can therefore mislead without this distinction.

The tradeoff register intentionally includes both successful design choices and shortcuts that reduce robustness.

**Descriptive name:** **ns-3 Moving-STA Wi-Fi Throughput Experiment**

A compact ns-3 C++ simulation with one 802.11n AP and one station moving at 4 m/s, a high-rate UDP client/server flow, MinstrelHT rate control, FlowMonitor statistics and one-second scheduled throughput reporting. It directly connects mobility and Wi-Fi performance in code. However, the periodic “throughput vs time” value divides cumulative received bytes by cumulative elapsed time, so it is a running-average throughput rather than true per-interval instantaneous throughput. The default channel/environment and single-run topology also limit research conclusions.
